11.0.0.en: 1 Then she prospered their works by the hand of a holy prophet. 2 They journeyed through a wilderness that was uninhabited, and pitched their tents in a desolate land, 3 and they withstood those who fought against them, and repelled their enemies.

11.0.1.en: And she made their endeavors prosper by the hand of a holy prophet. [1]

11.0.2.en: After speaking of the work of wisdom in the life of the early Fathers, he now records for us her work with the people under the leadership of Moses, "a holy prophet," the leader of the march of the Exodus. As it was said of him: "If there be a prophet among you, I the LORD will make myself known unto him in a vision, and will speak unto him in a dream. My servant Moses is not so, who is faithful in all mine house. With him will I speak mouth to mouth, even apparently, and not in dark speeches; and the similitude of the LORD shall he behold" (Num 12:6-8).

11.0.3.en: Just as he avoided mentioning the names of the righteous before, here too he avoided the name of Moses the holy prophet.

11.0.4.en: In every age God sends leaders whose hearts are aflame with the Spirit, who work continually for the sake of the Kingdom of God. God chooses the suitable leader for every age, and equips him with qualities and abilities that suit the circumstances of the age. So He sent Moses to lead the people on the journey of the Exodus. And God prepared Joshua as a type of Jesus Christ, to bring them into the land of promise, and raised up David to repair what Saul had spoiled, and prepared Solomon for the building of the temple, and sent St. Athanasius to resist Arius, and St. Cyril the Great to resist Nestorius.

11.0.5.en: * After Moses was given authority from the Theophany (the vision of God) that appeared to him, he received a command to deliver his Hebrew countrymen from the bondage of the Egyptians. And in order to be more fully assured of the power God had placed in him, he tested the divine command by the things in his hands (Ex 4:1-7), for when the rod fell from his hand, life stirred in it, and when he took hold of it with his hand again, it returned to what it had been. And when he drew his hand out of his bosom, it became leprous as snow, and when he put it a second time into his bosom, it returned to its natural color.

11.0.6.en: * After Moses gained strength from the light that was revealed to him, and his brother came as an ally and supporter to him, he boldly proclaimed to the people the good news of freedom, and reminded them of the greatness of their fathers. And he expressed his opinion about the way in which they could be delivered from the hard labor of making bricks (Ex 6).

11.1.s.en: What do we learn from this?

11.1.0.en: We must learn that whoever has not prepared himself by this kind of spiritual training to teach the multitudes should not speak to the people. For we see that when Moses was still young and had not yet matured and reached a high degree of virtue, the two men who were quarreling paid no heed to his sound advice and did not accept it. Yet after his descent from the mountain he addressed tens of thousands in the same manner.

11.1.1.en: The history of Moses shows us clearly that we must not dare to give advice to those who listen to us in our teaching of them unless the ability for it has been perfected in us by long and arduous training, as it was with Moses.

11.2.0.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa So they journeyed through an uninhabited wilderness, and pitched their tents in places that no foot had trodden. [2]

11.2.1.en: The true leader of the journey of the Exodus was the wisdom of God, for neither the people nor the leader had previous experience in the journey of a people through a desolate wilderness, so there were no guarantees, on a fearful, empty road with no trace of life.

11.2.2.en: They faced on their journey mighty enemies such as Amalek and others, and they were not men of war, nor did they have weapons, so the victory came as a divine gift presented to them.

11.2.3.en: He also avoided mentioning certain names such as Aaron and Miriam and others, for what the wisdom of God offered was for the whole congregation if it is sanctified in the Lord.

11.3.0.en: And they withstood those who fought against them, and repelled their enemies. [3]

11.3.1.en: There is no point of comparison between a people that lived in bondage, that had never practiced military life, and had no weapons, and strong enemies experienced in fighting. But the wisdom of God, or the Word of God, was the hidden leader, the giver of victory.

11.4.s.en: 2. The first contrast: water for death in Egypt and another for life in the wilderness

11.4.0.en: 4 And in their thirst they called upon You; and water was given them out of flinty rock, and a quenching of their thirst from the hard stone. 5 So that by which their enemies were tormented, when they lacked what to drink, while the children of Israel rejoiced in its abundance, 6 was the very thing by which kindness was shown them in their need. 7 For You confounded those, in that You changed for them the perennial fountain of the river into foul blood, 8 as a punishment for their decreeing the killing of infants, and to these You gave abundant water when they had despaired of it, 9 that You might show them by this thirst of theirs how You punished their adversaries.

11.4.1.en: When they thirsted they called upon You, and water was given them out of flinty rock, and a quenching of their thirst from the hard stone. [4]

11.4.2.en: The water was spent from their vessels in the midst of a barren desert, these who had lived all their days relying on the waters of the Nile, and by human reasoning there was no way of life; but the wisdom of God worked, and a spring of water bursting forth from a hard rock that accompanied them was granted to them (Ex 17:1-7; Num 20:2-13), without human effort. For He did not require them to dig wells from which to drink. This free gift is beyond price, for it is a matter of life or death; a matter of the existence of the people or their destruction. Therefore this rock became a type of the Lord Christ, the Giver of resurrection. "And did all drink the same spiritual drink: for they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ" (1 Cor 10:4).

11.4.3.en: Since the writer wants us to thirst for the water of life, and so to drink from the springs of the love of the Lord Christ, the wisdom of God, he fixed our eyes on the people's recourse to God that they might be refreshed, and did not point to their murmuring (Ex 17:2-3), and that they almost stoned Moses.

11.4.4.en: What occupies the writer is not the historical presentation of events, but fixing our eyes on the wisdom of God so that we may not lack anything.

11.4.5.en: The Evangelist describes for us the Lord Christ's call to all mankind to come to Him and drink, as he says: "Jesus stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink. He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water. But this spake he of the Spirit, which they that believe on him should receive" (Jn 7:37-39). By saying "if any man thirst" He opens the door for all, to come and drink.

11.5.0.en: For the things by which their enemies were punished became those by which kindness was shown to them in their distress. [5]

11.5.1.en: God punished the unbelieving Egyptians with the waters that were polluted with blood (Ex 7:24), and saved His people with pure waters bursting forth from the rock in the wilderness. The Nile, which is counted a source of life, became a source of death, and the wilderness, which is counted a cause of destruction, offered life. The water became a punishment for those who rejected the wisdom of God, and a blessing for those who enjoy wisdom. So what was a punishment for their enemies became for His people a sign of God's care for them and His concern for them, for He gave them water, not from the river Nile, but from a solid rock.

11.5.2.en: We can also say that in the waters of Baptism the devil, the enemy of good, loses his authority and his kingdom is shattered, and in the very same waters the baptized enjoys sonship to God.

11.5.3.en: * At the command of Moses all the waters in Egypt were turned into blood (Ex 7:20-22), and the fish died on account of the thickening of the waters, but for the Hebrews the water remained as it was. And the magicians seized the opportunity to use their art to make the water that had not turned into blood, which was with the Hebrews, appear as though it were blood.

11.5.4.en: * Whoever possesses the rod of virtue that is not defeated, which swallows up the rod of the magicians, advances to training in greater wonders. And the wonders do not happen to terrify those present, but for the benefit of those who are being rescued. For through the wonders of virtue the enemy is defeated and the people are strengthened.

11.5.5.en: If we first know the general spiritual purpose of the wonders of virtue, we can then apply this understanding to each miracle in itself. And true faith agrees with the inclinations of those who hear the word; for although the word shows everyone what is good and what is evil, yet the person with good inclinations toward what he hears has his understanding enlightened, while the words of ignorance remain overshadowing the person of stubborn inclinations, who does not allow his spirit to see the ray of truth. And if our general understanding of these matters is not mistaken, then each matter in itself will not appear different, since the part is shown and made clear by the whole.

11.5.6.en: Therefore it is not at all strange that the Hebrew, though living in the midst of strangers, is not affected by the evil of the Egyptians. We can see the same thing happening now in cities crowded with people whose opinions contradict one another. For some, the river of faith from which they drink through the divine teaching is sweet and pure, while for others who live like the Egyptians and drink with their evil passions, the water becomes for them foul blood.

11.5.7.en: And many times the master of evil and deceit tries to turn the water of the Hebrews also into blood by corrupting it with fraud and falsehood, that is, by showing us our doctrine otherwise than as it truly is; but he cannot corrupt the water so completely that it is not fit for use at all, even if he easily turned it red by his deceit, for the Hebrew, who pays no heed to the optical illusion, drinks the real water, even if his adversaries succeed in misleading him.

11.5.8.en: * Once again the cloud rose and led them to another place (Ex 17:1-7). But this place was a barren desert with burning sands, and there was not a drop of water in it. And here again thirst wearied the people. But when Moses struck a projecting rock with his rod, it brought forth sweet water, fit to drink, in greater abundance than all this great multitude needed.

11.6.0.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa And instead of the fountain of a perennial river, troubled with corrupt blood. [6]

11.6.1.en: God gave them a river with its sweet waters, but by their corruption its water became corrupt, and became a source of destruction to them, not a source of life. So God gave us His commandment as a sweet yoke, but by the evil of our will the yoke becomes heavy, and the good commandment turns into a cause of our condemnation and our destruction.

11.6.2.en: * How then does the wonderful sweetness of the yoke of Christ become bitter except because of the bitterness of our evil? How does the very light divine burden become heavy, except that in our stubborn insolence we despise the Lord by whom we bear His burden, especially since Scripture itself clearly bears witness to this, saying: "His own iniquities shall take the wicked himself, and he shall be holden with the cords of his sins" (Prov 22:5; Wis 11:16)?

11.6.3.en: I say it is clear that we are the ones who make the easy, sound ways of the Lord into wearisome ways, because of the heavy stones of our evil lusts, for in folly we make the royal road a stony ground, and we leave the road that the feet of all the saints have trodden, indeed in which the Lord Himself walked, seeking a road with no footprints of those who went before us, seeking places full of thorns, so the allurements of present delights blind us, and the wedding garment is torn by the thorns in the darkness... And the road has been covered with rods of sins, so that we are not only torn by the sharp thorns of the bramble, but are cast down by the bites of deadly serpents and of vipers lurking there, for "thorns and snares are in the way of the froward" (Prov 5:22).

11.6.4.en: The Lord says in another place through the prophet: "Because my people hath forgotten me... and they have caused them to stumble in their ways from the ancient paths, to walk in paths, in a way not cast up" (Jer 15:18). And Solomon says: "The way of the slothful man is as an hedge of thorns" (Prov 19:15). So when they go astray from the heavenly royal road, they are unable to reach the city on which our gaze was fixed. And the book of Ecclesiastes expressed it symbolically, saying of it that it is Jerusalem... (Eccl 15:10). That is, "Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all" (Gal 26:4).

11.6.5.en: But whoever truly leaves this world and takes the yoke of Christ and learns from Him, and trains himself daily to bear toil, because the Lord is "meek and lowly in heart" (Mt 29:11), remains continually undisturbed by all trials, and for him "all things work together for good" (Rom 28:8). As the prophet (Micah) says, the words of God are good to him who walks uprightly (Mic 2:7).

11.7.0.en: Father Abraham As a punishment for a command to kill infants, You gave them unexpectedly abundant water. [7]

11.7.1.en: The water flowing in the river Nile became a punishment for the Egyptians, for it became blood (Ex 7:17-21), because they shed the blood of many infants by the command of Pharaoh (Ex 1:8-10), so death threatened the Egyptians.

11.7.2.en: It is said in Exodus 7:14-24 that this plague came to urge Pharaoh to let the people of God go, but here he sees in this plague a chastisement for Pharaoh's decision to kill the infants of the Hebrews (Ex 1:16, 22). This plague can serve both purposes together.

11.7.3.en: * In the water the Egyptians used to kill the infants of the children of Israel, and by the water God began their torment, when He made it blood that they could not drink. He measured to them with the measure by which they had measured to others.

11.7.4.en: St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian * In fact the turning of the water of the river into blood was fitting. The river in which the infants of the Hebrews were cruelly drowned gave back to the perpetrators of that crime a cup of blood, and when they drank from it they were slain by the corrupt waters that they had defiled by wicked murder.

11.8.0.en: Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles After You had shown them by their thirst at that time how You punished their adversaries. [8]

11.8.1.en: If God allowed this plague for the Egyptians who resisted the truth, He also allowed the Hebrews to thirst in the midst of the wilderness so that they might experience for a while the bitterness of the plague that struck the Egyptians in depriving them of the pure water of the Nile, so that it might be a lesson for them in the midst of the wilderness.

11.9.0.en: For when they were tested, though it was a chastisement of mercy, they learned how the wicked were tormented, who were judged in wrath. [9]

11.9.1.en: God's chastening of His people is an instructive work full of mercy.

11.9.2.en: With God there is no partiality toward the Jews; He chastened the unbelieving Egyptians with the plague of the water that became blood, and the plagues followed one after another, revealing the hardness of their hearts and their insistence on not believing in God the Worker of wonders. As for the Jews, He allowed them the trial of thirst in order to chasten them in His mercy, and when Moses had recourse to God, He gave him water from the rock of Horeb.

11.10.s.en: 3. God the Father and the Ruler!

11.10.0.en: 10 For when they were tested by You, though it was a chastisement of mercy, they understood how the torment of the hypocrites, who were condemned in wrath, had been. 11 For You tried these as a father, admonishing them, and those You tested as a stern king, condemning them. 12 And the same distress touched them in absence as in presence, 13 for a twofold grief seized them, and groaning at the remembrance of past plagues, 14 for when they heard that what was a punishment to them had become kindness to their enemies, they felt the hand of the Lord. 15 And him whom they had before decreed to be cast into the river, and had despised and rejected, they marveled at in the end of the matter, for the thirst of the righteous was unlike their thirst.

11.10.1.en: For You tested these as a father admonishing them, and those You judged as a stern king condemning them. [10]

11.10.2.en: What befell the Egyptians was a punishment for restraint, while the thirst that befell the Hebrews was a fatherly chastisement for warning.

11.11.0.en: And whether they were absent or present, they suffered torment alike. [11]

11.11.1.en: Both parties suffered torment alike; thirst befell both parties, but the situation in each case was different from the other.

11.12.0.en: For a twofold grief seized them, and groaning at the remembrance of the past. [12]

11.12.1.en: In the presence of the Jews grief befell the Egyptians when the water turned into blood, and after the Jews departed to the wilderness their grief was doubled, for they saw those whom they had formerly enslaved having become a great people bearing surpassing power, overcoming the difficulties of the wilderness by the God of the impossible, who is able to provide them water from a solid rock that followed them on their journey.

11.12.2.en: Some see that the grief of the wicked is doubled: grief because of the chastisement that comes upon them, and another grief because of the blessings that are granted to those who trouble them and wrong them.

11.13.0.en: For when they heard that what was a punishment for them was a kindness to their enemies, they felt the hand of the Lord. [13]

11.14.0.en: For him whom they had cast out before, and rejected with mockery, they marveled at in the end of the matter, for their thirst was unlike the thirst of the righteous. [14]

11.14.1.en: It seems that all the nations surrounding the region - including Egypt - were following the events of the Exodus. So when the Egyptians heard of the thirst of the Hebrews and then of the bringing forth of water from the rock, they were amazed, and realized that they had previously mocked God through His people and rejected Him, which had destroyed their king and their army, while the Hebrews benefited from the thirst!

11.14.2.en: Moses the prophet, whom the Egyptians rejected and the Jews also, became the object of amazement to both.

11.14.3.en: Moses was an instrument that God used for the thirst of the Egyptians, and he himself became an instrument for quenching the thirst of the Israelites.

11.15.s.en: 4. God's forbearance in His dealing with Egypt

11.15.0.en: 16 And since they had been foolish in their wicked thoughts, and went astray so as to worship contemptible creeping things and beasts without speech, You took vengeance on them by sending upon them a multitude of creatures without speech, in return for the foolish, unjust thoughts which led them astray so that they worshiped serpents without speech and contemptible insects, You punished them by sending upon them a multitude of creatures without speech. [15]

11.15.1.en: Some forms of worship spread in ancient Egypt, such as the worship of the crocodile and the snakes and the fox and the ram (the god Amun), and the Apis bull and the lioness and the cow (the god Hathor) and the falcon, the ape, the hippopotamus, the cat, the frog and the serpent, as well as the beetle and the scarab (among insects).

11.15.2.en: As for the contemptible insect, perhaps what is meant is the scarab, which the ancient Egyptians exalted, so they engraved it on their rings and their ornaments and their gold.

11.15.3.en: The chastisement came from the same deed, for since they worshiped animals and reptiles and insects as gods, He struck them with insects and frogs that attacked their houses and entered into their chambers, and many of them died and stank, so they were asking to be rid of them (Ex 8:8).

11.15.4.en: The Egyptians were struck with three small animals or insects in the plagues 2, 3 and 4, which are the plagues of the frogs, the gnats and the flies.

11.15.5.en: As for the frogs: St. Augustine sees that they refer to those who speak much that is vain and unprofitable, and Origen sees that they refer to the songs of the poets, which are like the croaking of frogs, producing twisted, annoying sounds without work. And Isidore of Seville (died in the year 636) took this from him, as he says: [In the second plague the frogs were brought. And it is thought that they symbolize the songs of the poets who brought into this world flimsy, deceitful stories. By their empty songs full of vanity, like the croaking of frogs. For the frog produces empty chatter. This animal is of no use at all, but only produces annoying, loathsome sounds.]

11.15.6.en: And as for the gnats: the priests of the Egyptians were very careful about cleanliness and guarded against being defiled by gnats and lice. Origen sees that the gnats refer to sweetened words that deceive a person with cunning, so that he does not feel them during their deceiving, like gnats that sting and the person does not feel them except after the sting. Therefore Father Isidore of Seville sees that they refer to the heretics.

11.15.7.en: And as for the flies, God allowed them to reveal the helplessness of the gods of the Egyptians, since they believed that they drove away the flies. And Father Isidore says that the fly is an insolent insect that never rests, and God allowed the Egyptians to be struck with flies that they might realize that their world-loving hearts are struck with the disturbance of passions that never cease.

11.16.s.en: 5. The second contrast: quails in the wilderness against the plague of insects.

11.16.0.en: 17 That they might know that by what things a man sins, by the same he is punished. 18 For it was not difficult for Your hand, which is almighty, which made the world out of formless matter, to send upon them a multitude of bears or bold lions, 19 or new kinds of unknown ravenous beasts, breathing out fire, or sending forth a dark smoke, or flashing dreadful sparks from their eyes. 20 Then they would have destroyed them by fear at their appearance, let alone crushing them by their attack. 21 Yea, a breath was enough to cast them down; justice would pursue them, and the spirit of Your power scatter them. But You have ordered all things in measure and number and weight.

11.16.1.en: That they might know that every one is punished by that by which he sinned. [16]

11.16.2.en: The insects came upon the Egyptians in return for their worship of animals such as the crocodile, the snake, the lizard and the frog. For this they were struck with the frogs (Ex 8:1-15), the gnats (Ex 8:16-19), the flies (Ex 8:20-24), and the locusts (Ex 10:3-15).

11.16.3.en: He links the vain gods, their worshipers and their chastisements. For since they were foolish - without reason - they worshiped irrational animals, and fell under chastisement by irrational animals or insects. So worshipers share with their gods in their characteristics. Whoever worships vain gods becomes vain himself, and whoever worships the Lover of mankind and its Savior becomes a lover of men, and desires to be given for the sake of everyone.

11.16.4.en: In this passage the writer affirms that the punishment (or chastisement) comes upon the wicked by the very things by which he sinned. For since the Egyptians worshiped animals instead of God, the plagues came upon them by animals and insects.

11.16.5.en: * It is not easy to decide whether we should despise the worshipers of them or the things that are the object of worship. The more likely is the worshipers, for they are more trivial, because they are of a rational nature and received grace from God, yet they set up the worse instead of the better. And this is the deceit of the evil one, who corrupted what is good to be used for an evil purpose, and that in most of his evil works.

11.16.6.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus And it was not hard for Your all-powerful hand, which made the world out of formless matter, to send upon them a multitude of bears, or bold lions. [17]

11.16.7.en: It is God's care even for the wicked, for He could have destroyed the Egyptians at once by sending upon them bears and lions that devour them, but He sent small insects that trouble them without killing them, in order to chasten them. He did not desire their destruction and death, but seeks their repentance and their life.

11.16.8.en: The Creator of the world out of an empty and void earth (Gen 1:2) is able to punish by sending ravenous and terrifying beasts, as happened in Samaria (2 Kgs 17:26).

11.16.9.en: * Although He created things out of things, as He created man from the dust, yet the earth from which the dust came He created out of nothing.

11.17.0.en: St. Augustine Or ravenous beasts unknown and newly created, full of wrath, either breathing out a fiery blast or belching forth a foul smoke, or sending forth dreadful sparks from their eyes. [18]

11.17.1.en: Again he says that there was no need to send fierce, savage animals to devour them, nor to create new terrifying animals that destroy them by their frightening sight, but one breath is enough, and all fall and do not rise.

11.17.2.en: In His justice He could have pursued them with a breath from His mouth; He says a word that issues a sentence of death upon them and they die. But God does not desire to destroy, but to chasten in due measure.

11.18.0.en: Then they would have destroyed them by fear at their appearance, let alone crushing them by their harm. [19]

11.18.1.en: Even without these animals, one breath was enough to cast them down, justice pursuing them and scattering them by the breath of Your power.

11.19.0.en: But You have ordered all things in measure and number and weight. [20]

11.19.1.en: God the Creator was able to create new beasts that would destroy them, not only by devouring them, but also by the terror that comes upon them from their sight, as it is said of Medusa, who used to destroy people by her terrifying appearance. For even in His chastening of the wicked He does so with wisdom, in measure and number and weight, that is, by an exact divine ordering, and for a purpose in God's mind toward them, without compelling them to return to Him by force.

11.19.2.en: God is a God of order, not of confusion (1 Cor 14:33); all that He does is with exactness and surpassing divine ordering.

11.19.3.en: * Every creature, great or small, was made by Him. In Him were created things above and things below, spiritual and material. So there is no form, nor arrangement of parts, nor any matter whatever, of whatever weight or number or measure, that exists except by that Word the Creator, to whom it was said: "You have ordered all things in measure and number and weight" (Wis 11:20).

11.19.4.en: * In the books of our Scripture it is said to God: "You have ordered all things in measure and number and weight" (Wis 11:21). The prophet also says: "He calleth them all (the host of heaven) by names" (Isa 40:26). And the Savior says in the Gospel: "But the very hairs of your head are all numbered" (Mt 10:30).

11.19.5.en: * We do not know the number of the saints or the number of the demons, but we know that the children of the holy mother who was called barren on earth (the Church) will occupy the place of the fallen angels, and will dwell forever in that abode full of peace from which they fell. As for the number of the citizens, whether at present or as it will be, it is present in the thoughts of the great Creator, He who called things that are not into being (Rom 4:7), and orders all things by measure and number and weight (Wis 11:20).

11.19.6.en: St. Augustine St. Augustine also sees that if God in His unlimited knowledge orders everything by a certain number that He knows perfectly, then it is fitting for us to pay attention to the numbers mentioned in Holy Scripture, and to know their symbolic spiritual meanings.

11.19.7.en: St. Augustine sees that man in his spiritual life may walk in a particular order, through four stages that correspond to the four stages of the history of the Church. In the first stage man is like one in the depth of ignorance, not knowing what he is; the second stage is when he knows sin through the Law, so he feels that he is overcome by sin and a slave to it (Rom 5:5), and as the Apostle says, the Law entered that the offence might abound (Rom 5:20). And when God grants him faith he receives the power of love, so he struggles against the lusts of the flesh, and lives righteous by faith, and is counted righteous as long as he does not submit to evil desire, but overcomes it by his love of holiness. This is the third stage, of good hope. Whoever holds fast to this finally receives in the fourth stage peace, especially at the end when the body rises glorified. These four stages correspond to the stages of the history of the Church. The first stage is before the Law, the second under the Law, the third in the age of grace when the Savior came, and then the fourth in the resurrection.

11.20.0.en: 22 And You have great power at all times; who can resist the strength of Your arm? 23 For the whole world before You is as what tips the balance of the scales, and as a drop of dew that falls upon the earth at dawn. 24 But You have mercy on all, because You are able to do all things, and You overlook the sins of men that they may repent. 25 For You love all existing things, and loathe nothing that You made; for You would not have formed anything You hated. 26 And how could anything endure if You had not willed it? Or how would what was not called by You be preserved? 27 You spare all things, for they are Yours, O Lord who love souls.

11.20.1.en: For Your great power is always at Your disposal; who can resist the strength of Your arm? [21]

11.20.2.en: There is no point of comparison between the great power of God and the power of man, for the power of God has its source not outside Himself, but He bears in Himself His strength and power, therefore it is at His disposal, He uses it as He wills. But the power of man is not from himself, but is a gift presented to him that will surely depart from him one day. For if he is struck with sickness or poverty or loses his social position, his strength departs with it or grows weak, and he becomes feeble. Many have had their arms and their spirits shattered, but as for God the Almighty, there is no one who can resist His arm!

11.20.3.en: Often man wrongs God because of his inability to know God's plan and thoughts, so he ascribes to Him weakness because of His long-suffering, or inability because of the tribulations and persecutions that He allows to come upon His Church or His children. He is the Almighty, able to do everything with surpassing power, but how unsearchable are His judgments, and His ways past finding out? (Rom 11:33); "for who hath known the mind of the Lord? or who hath been his counsellor?" (Rom 11:34).

11.20.4.en: It is said in the supplication of Mordecai to God: "You are Lord of all, and there is none who can resist Your might" (Add Esth 13:11). Judith says: "Who are you that you should tempt the Lord?" (Jdt 8:11). And the Apostle Paul says: "Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God? Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why hast thou made me thus?" (Rom 9:20).

11.20.5.en: For the whole world before You is as what tips the balance of the scales, and as a drop of the dew of the dawn that falls upon the earth. [22]

11.20.6.en: "Behold, the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance" (Isa 40:15). He likens God to one who holds a balance to put the whole world in one pan, and behold, it is like a drop of morning dew or the dust of the balance. And on the other hand He puts the whole world in one pan and man in the other pan, and there is no point of comparison or balance between them. God presents His love to man with great exactness, according to what is for his edification.

11.20.7.en: * On this hope our souls cleave to Him who is faithful in His promises, just in His judgments.

11.20.8.en: He who commanded us not to lie will not lie, for there is nothing that is impossible to Him except lying.

11.20.9.en: Let our faith be kindled within us that we may realize that everything is near to Him.

11.20.10.en: For by the word of His power He established all, and by His word He is able to destroy everything.

11.20.11.en: "Who shall say to Him, What have You done? Who can resist the strength of His authority?" (Wis 12:12; 11:22). He does what He wills and as He wills, and nothing opposes His command.

11.21.0.en: St. Clement of Rome But You have mercy on all, because You are able to do all things, and You overlook the sins of men that they may repent. [23]

11.21.1.en: The mercy of God embraces all creation, for it is His work, so how much more does He show kindness to man, for whose sake He created all things. God is a lover of mankind even in His chastenings of them, for their goal is repentance (metanoia), which He seeks from all sinners, and not from a particular nation, for His door is open to all.

11.21.2.en: His view of mankind is wonderful, for men are the good creation of God, but their choice of evil isolates them from God, the source of their goodness. Therefore God continues to call them to repentance, that is, to return to Him, for they are the object of His love and mercy.

11.21.3.en: "You overlook" here means "You are long-suffering," for He does not will that men should perish, but that all should come to repentance (2 Pet 3:9). And when we return to Him in repentance, He says that He no longer remembers our sins.

11.22.0.en: For You love all things that exist, and loathe nothing that You made; for You would not have formed anything You hated. [24]

11.22.1.en: God is Almighty, and cannot be resisted, and He is love itself toward all heavenly and earthly beings. By this view He prepares man to receive free salvation from God who loves the whole world by giving the only-begotten Son (Jn 3:16).

11.22.2.en: * The heavenly Father knows what we need before we ask Him (Mt 6:8). It is reasonable that He who is the Father of the world and its Creator, who loves all beings and loathes nothing that He made (Wis 11:24), provides what is for the benefit of each one without prayer to Him; He does this as a father who protects his little ones and does not wait for them to ask Him, whether they are altogether unable to ask Him, or because of their ignorance, for they often ask for what is entirely against their benefit.

11.22.3.en: Origen St. Augustine asks: If God hates nothing that He made, how was it said that He hated Esau? He answers this, saying: [God is the maker of all creatures. Every creature of God is good. Every man is a creature as man, not as a sinner. God is the Creator of both the body of man and his soul. Neither of them is evil, and God does not hate them. He hates nothing in man but sin. Sin in man is a distortion and disorder, that is, a straying from the Creator, who is the highest (from the soul), and a resort to the creatures lower than He (the lusts of the flesh and the love of the world, etc.). God hates Esau not as man, but as sinner.]

11.22.4.en: * The love with which God loves is beyond comprehension and unchanging. For He did not begin to love us from the time when we were reconciled to Him by the blood of His Son, but He loved us even before the foundation of the world, that we might become sons to Him with His only-begotten Son; He loved us even before there was any existence of ours. Let us not look at the reality of our reconciliation with God through the death of His Son, nor understand it as though the reconciliation of the Son to us with Him were accomplished in this manner: that He has now begun to love those whom He formerly hated, as though an enemy were reconciled with an enemy, and they became friends, and mutual love took the place of mutual hatred. Rather we were reconciled with Him who was already loving us, but we ourselves had become enemies because of our sins.

11.22.5.en: That you may realize that I speak the truth in this, let the Apostle bear witness, who says: "God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us" (Rom 5:8). So God bears love for us even when we were practicing enmity against Him, and doing iniquity.

11.22.6.en: It was said to Him with perfect truth: "Thou hatest all workers of iniquity" (Ps 5:5). So in a wonderful divine way, when we hated Him, He loved us. For He hated us in what we were, which He had not created us to be... He hates what we have made of ourselves, and loves what He has made in us!

11.22.7.en: This can be understood truly in the case of all, concerning Him to whom it was said with truth: "You hate nothing that You made" (Wis 11:24).

11.23.0.en: St. Augustine And how could anything endure that You had not willed, or how be preserved if not called by You? [25]

11.23.1.en: Here the wonder of the love of God is brought out, for He created man that he might remain with Him, keeping him from every danger. For God wants man and loves him and protects him from every harm, and prepares a place for him in heaven.

11.23.2.en: * If there is a rich woman who possesses much wealth and a splendid house, yet finds no one to protect her, for many attack her wishing to inflict harm and ruin upon her. And because she cannot bear this harm and attack, she therefore seeks a strong husband who would be equal to this purpose, and trained in all respects. And when she finds such a man after much seeking, she rejoices in him greatly, and finds in him a fortress that protects her.

11.24.0.en: You spare all things, for they are Yours, O Lord, lover of the living. [26]

11.24.1.en: The purpose of His creating man and the goal of it is man's being with God, as the son who rests in the bosom of his father full of tenderness toward him.

11.24.2.en: God is life; He possesses man for Himself and grants him life.

11.24.3.en: * God rules all creation (the earthly), but He did not establish His throne in it, nor did He enter into fellowship with it, but He was pleased with man alone, and entered into fellowship with him, and in him alone He rested... The wise soul, after passing through all creatures, finds no rest for itself except in the Lord alone, and the Lord also is not pleased with anyone but man alone.

11.24.5.en: Grant me Your wisdom, that I may perceive the mysteries of Your love!

11.24.6.en: * Your wisdom raised up a leader for Your people.

11.24.7.en: You gave them a holy prophet who works by Your Spirit!

11.24.8.en: Moses in his youth thought that he was able to save Your people!

11.24.9.en: In weakness he could not reconcile two brothers of Your enslaved people!

11.24.10.en: But Your wisdom supported him when he was an old man of eighty.

11.24.11.en: Wisdom moved him and renewed his inner youth.

11.24.12.en: He defied the violence of Pharaoh and the harshness of the wilderness.

11.24.13.en: The old man overcame kings, and enjoyed wonderful blessings!

11.24.14.en: Your wisdom, O my God, is able to raise up a hero from the weak!

11.24.15.en: Your wisdom shepherds Your people, and cares for every believer!

11.24.16.en: Your wisdom is the Good Shepherd, who raises up leaders from among the believers.

11.24.17.en: * Your people collapsed from thirst in the midst of the wilderness.

11.24.18.en: So waters burst forth for them from a flinty rock.

11.24.19.en: And they saw in it Your wisdom, which makes burst forth in its belly - the hard stones - springs of living waters of love.

11.24.20.en: The unbelievers were deprived of wisdom, so the Nile offered them corrupt water mixed with the blood of the infants that they had shed!

11.24.21.en: And the believers enjoyed wisdom, so springs of living water burst forth in them!

11.24.22.en: The water of the Nile turned for the unbelievers into blood, and the water of the rock refreshed the believers and prepared them for life in the wilderness.

11.24.23.en: The unbelievers thirsted and died, and the believers thirsted and experienced life by You and with You!

11.24.24.en: * Without partiality You chasten; grant me to accept Your chastening from Your life-giving hands, that I may taste Your fatherhood, and respond to Your love for me.

11.24.25.en: That I may see You a Father who chastens in order to give life, and not a judge who punishes because You cannot bear sin.

11.24.26.en: * The wicked are troubled and grieve, for they count in their chastening a harshness that comes from You.

11.24.27.en: And Your righteous ones see You and rejoice in the midst of affliction, and experience Your love.

11.24.28.en: * You are wonderful, O wisdom of God, in Your tenderness, even with the wicked You are gentle and compassionate, You chasten and punish, but little by little.

11.24.29.en: For You created man, not to destroy him but to give him life.

11.24.30.en: You wait even for the wicked to return to You.

11.24.31.en: In firmness You chasten, that perhaps they may return to themselves, seek You and live.

11.24.32.en: * The ancient Egyptians worshiped animals and reptiles and insects.

11.24.33.en: From the kinds of their gods You punished them by their very sins, that sin might become bitter in their mouths.

11.24.34.en: You could have sent upon them beasts to devour them.

11.24.35.en: Or destroyed them with a word from Your mouth.

11.24.36.en: But You do not will the death of the sinner, but that he should return and live.

11.24.37.en: You sent them insects to trouble them, not to kill them.

11.24.38.en: For even while You chasten, You spare!

11.24.39.en: For Your creation is very dear to You.

11.24.40.en: Glory to You, O Lover of all mankind!
